list.listitem: If the patient is not ovulating, correct the cause if possible. Proceed with ovulation induction with letrozole, clomiphene, metformin, or both clomiphene and metformin. A If unsuccessful, consider referral for injectable hormonal therapy. C
If there is intrauterine disease, consider operative hysteroscopy. C

If there is tubal blockage distally, consider operative laparoscopy. For tubal blockage proximally, consider interventional radiology to relieve obstruction. C Tubal flushing with oil-soluble contrast media may increase live birth rates. B
If work-up is negative and the patient wishes to defer laparoscopy, consider trial of intrauterine insemination (IUI) and clomiphene or letrozole. B
Refer for in vitro fertilization (IVF) when appropriate (e.g., severe tubal disease, need for donor eggs, sophisticated sperm manipulation, refractory ovulation, failed IUI). C

background.definition: Infertility is failure to conceive after 1 year of appropriately-timed unprotected intercourse.

list.listitem: Increases with age: 14% at ages 30 to 34 years, 20% at ages 35 to 39 years, and 25% at ages 40 to 45 years.
Incidence of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in reproductive-age women is 5% to 10%; about 70% of women with anovulation have PCOS.
Ten to fifteen percent of all couples.

In a 2014 study of 332 couples recruited from 8 community and academic reproductive endocrinology clinics, overall out-of-pocket expenses ranged from $912 for those using medication only to $19,234 for those using in vitro fertilization. About $6955 was spent for each additional in vitro fertilization cycle.
Incidence is increasing because 20% of women are delaying childbearing until after age 35 years.
Up to 50% of women with endometriosis are infertile.
Women with infertility appear to be at increased risk of ovarian malignancy; there is no proven relationship between use of fertility drugs and ovarian malignancy, although data are conflicting.
Women with infertility also have an increased risk of having celiac disease (pooled seroprevalence 1.3% to 1.6% vs. population risk of about 0.8%).

Major depression is common among couples who fail to conceive; in one cohort study of 174 women and 144 of their male partners who did not have a successful child-related outcome during the 18-month study period, 39.1% of the women and 15.3% of the men met the criteria for major depressive disorder. Authors of a review of studies on female infertility also found increased depression risk in 4 of 6 studies identified and increased anxiety diagnosis and psychosocial distress in 5 of the 6 studies.

Authors of a systemic review reported up to one-third of couples seen in tertiary fertility clinics were diagnosed with unexplained infertility - a diagnosis of exclusion for couples unable to conceive and do not meet criteria for a diagnosis of infertility due to ovulatory dysfunction, anatomical abnormalities, or male factor infertility.

Most couples have more than 1 cause: Tubal/peritoneal factors including endometriosis (40%) Male factors (30%-40%) Ovulation factors (15%) Cervical/uterine factors (10%) Immunologic factors (5%) Psychogenic/nutritional/metabolic factors (5%) Unexplained infertility (10%-20%; up to one third in tertiary clinics)

Infection In one small study of 40 women from India with secondary infertility, evidence of past infection with chlamydia (IgG) was found in 55% and current chlamydia infection (ELISA) in 12%. Similarly, the mean prevalence of gonorrhea appears to be higher in infertile populations than in the general population - 3.6% (95% CI 0.9%-7.7%) in those with tubal factor infertility, 3.6% (95% CI 0%-11.6%) for mixed cause and unexplained infertility, and 2.2% (95% CI 1.3%-3.2%) in the general population. Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies found that women with infertility had a statistically higher odds of having a genital mycoplasma infection compared to controls (pooled OR 3.82; 95% CI 2.55-5.72). In a second meta-analysis of 6 studies with 11,869 participants, there was a significant association between high-risk human papilloma virus infection and infertility (OR 2.33; 95% CI 1.42-3.83).

Caffeine more than2 cups per day
Excessive exercise in women with normal BMI

list.listitem: Maintain normal BMI; if overweight, loss of just 5% to 10% of body weight may be beneficial. A
Prevent sexually-transmitted infections (STIs) and subsequent PID. C
Discontinue or avoid smoking, alcohol, illicit drugs, and toxins both in the home and at work. B
Consider cryopreservation of oocytes or embryos for females undergoing gonadotoxic therapy or gonadectomy. C
Maintain normal BMI; if overweight, loss of just 5% to 10% of body weight may be beneficial.
Prevent STIs and subsequent PID.
Treat endometriosis when the diagnosis is made (e.g., oral contraceptive) to protect from disease progression.

Gonadotopin releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues are effective in reducing amenorrhea rates in patients undergoing chemotherapy (RR 0.26; 95% CI, 0.14-0.49) and pregnancy rate appears higher in the GnRH analogue arm, but this advantage was shown only in observational studies not in RCTs.

Authors of a Cochrane review based on 32 RCTs with 3492 women concluded that intraoperative use of gels or hydroflotation agents was effective for preventing postoperative adhesion formation but found no evidence that these agents improve fertility outcomes. Similarly, authors of a systematic review of 19 small RCTs on prophylactic use of barrier agents (e.g., fibrin or collagen sheets) during pelvic surgery found no evidence supporting a positive effect on live birth rates as this outcome was not evaluated.

Women preparing to have cancer treatment that is likely to result in fertility problems should consider cryopreservation of oocytes or embryos. The American Society of Reproductive Medicine opinion paper concludes that counseling should be provided to review options (principally embryo or oocyte preservation for females) for fertility preservation with rapid referral to an appropriate program. For prepubertal patients, ovarian tissue cryopreservation can be used, and for women undergoing pelvic radiation, ovarian transposition may be offered. GnRH agonists can be offered to women with breast cancer and potentially other cancers to protect from ovarian insufficiency, but GnRH analogs should not replace oocyte or embryo cryopreservation for fertility preservation.
Verify ovulation by reviewing menstrual history and consider obtaining serum progesterone 1 week prior to anticipated menses.

Infertility evaluation should include a semen analysis and comprehensive history and physical exam, with a focus on menstrual history, past infections, sexual dysfunction, surgical history, and medication use. C
Laboratory evaluation may include serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Imaging modalities to consider include hysterosalpingogram and pelvic ultrasound. B
Base additional work-up on history, physical examination, and results of initial testing. C

Abnormal BMI, elevated fasting glucose, possible elevation in fasting insulin
Elevated day 3 FSH (FSH <15 mIU/mL indicates adequate ovarian reserve)

list.listitem: Questions to ask when obtaining the history: Has the patient had genital or pelvic infections? There may be an obstruction within the reproductive tract. Has there been any evidence of endocrine dysfunction such as hypothyroidism, goiter, fatigue, prolactinoma, galactorrhea, or abnormal puberty? These conditions are associated with abnormalities of ovulation or spermatogenesis. Is there sexual dysfunction (e.g., premature ejaculation)? Are the cycles regular or not, and have they always been so? What has the pattern been since menarche? Have they varied with the patient's weight? Is there molimina (cramps, breast tenderness, uterine cramps) with each cycle? If no, consider anovulation. Is there any hirsutism or acne? Check the chin, face, intermammary areas, the escutcheon (pattern of distribution of pubic hair); consider PCOS. Are the periods very painful to the point of incapacity? If yes, consider endometriosis or uterine pathology. Premenstrual spotting of 2 or more days was strongly associated with endometriosis in one study of subfertile women (OR 16; 95% CI, 3.9-65.4). Has the patient initiated any new medications or herbal supplements (e.g., exogenous steroid use in males)?

Additional items to consider on physical examination: HEENT: note presence of exophthalmos, or lid lag; look for enlarged, tender, or nodular thyroid gland. Breasts: check for breast pain, masses, or galactorrhea; if nipple discharge, note color and consistency of secretion and if it is spontaneous or induced through significant manipulation. Abdominal and pelvic examination: presence of masses, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, enlarged lymph nodes, suprapubic masses, or tenderness in the lower quadrants (chronic illness can impair fertility). Check for Bartholin's gland abscesses; vulvitis; vaginitis; mucopurulent cervicitis; cervical motion tenderness; enlarged, irregular, or tender uterus; enlarged or tender adnexa; tenderness on rectal examination; and nodularity in the posterior cul-de-sac and the rectovaginal septum.

Confirm ovulatory function via the following methods: Serum progesterone approximately 1 week prior to expected onset of menses as opposed to any one specific day of the cycle (level > 3ng/mL presumes evidence of recent ovulation) Urinary luteinizing hormone (LH) using over-the-counter ovulation "predictor kits" may identify the mid-cycle LH surge prior to ovulation within 1-2 days. However, patients with PCOS may have elevated basal LH levels, resulting in false-positive elevations in urinary LH. Transvaginal ultrasound (see "Imaging" below). Daily basal body tempurature (BBT) measurement is no longer routinely recommended to confirm ovulatory function due to the tedious nature of testing and lack of accuracy. Endometrial biopsy has historically been used to document secretory endothelium, implying recent ovulation. However, histologic endometrial dating does not appear to be a valid clinical diagnostic tool for identification of infertility or for the diagnosis of luteal phase deficiency and is no longer recommended in routine infertility evaluation.
Order a sperm count to assess number and morphology using modified strict Krueger criteria.
For unexplained infertility, consider a trial of clomiphene citrate/IUI before operative laparoscopy and tubal insufflation.

Routine measurement of prolactin or thyroid hormones is not recommended. Specific signs and symptoms that direct further investigation include: Galactorrhea or amenorrhea: order prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) followed by MRI of pituitary if abnormality suggested. History of infection: check ultrasound to rule out gross hydrosalpinx, then order hysterosalpingogram (HSG). An intracervical block can be offered to women undergoing HSG to reduce procedural pain. In one RCT, pregnancy and live birth rates were significantly higher when oil-based contrast vs. water-based contrast was used with HSG (live birth rate 214 of 552 women [38.8%] vs. 155 of 552 women [28.1%], respectively). History of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility: consider laparoscopy to look for endometriosis. Hirsutism and acne: order free testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS), prolactin, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and pelvic ultrasound to evaluate for PCOS. Anovulation: consider work-up for PCOS, as above, FSH (premature ovarian failure), and fasting blood sugar.
The postcoital test is only of historical value; it is an attempt to assess sperm and cervical mucus interaction and is no longer recommended as part of infertility evaluation.

The American College of Radiology appropriateness criteria for infertility recommend pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal or transabdominal) for evaluation of ovulatory function and reserve, and transvaginal pelvic ultrasound as initial imaging for women with features or a history of PCOS. For women with a history or clinical suspicion of endometriosis, they recommend initial imaging with transvaginal, transabdominal, and/or transrectal pelvic ultrasound or MRI of the pelvis without IV contrast. When there is suspicion of tubal occlusion, fluoroscopy hysterosalpingography, ultrasound sonohysterography with tubal contrast agent, or pelvic transvaginal ultrasound are considered appropriate.
Sonohysterography (SHG) may demonstrate tubal patency; however, this test does not differentiate between unilateral or bilateral tubal patency.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies concluded that magnetic resonance hysterosalpingography for fallopian tubal occlusion was comparable to conditional X-ray hysterosalpingography.

Use pelvic ultrasound to assess for both intramural and submucosal fibroids, ovarian pathology including endometriomas and sub cortical ovarian cysts, Müllerian defects, and tubal pathology such as hydrosalpinx. An MRI can be used to assess for Müllerian defects with more accuracy, but only if suggested by the ultrasound.
Testicular ultrasound is not recommended in the setting of a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria.

Laparoscopy can be used to assess tubal patency, presence of endometriosis, and presence of adhesive disease; hysteroscopy is helpful to assess intrauterine pathology. HSG to assess tubal patency can be therapeutic.
Laparoscopy is not recommended for routine evaluation of infertility in the absence of suspected pelvic pathology or specific indication that would require surgical evaluation.
Hysteroscopy: Data are conflicting on usefulness of hysteroscopy prior to in vitro fertilization (IVF).

For women about to undergo intracytoplasmic sperm injection (see Drug Therapy), one RCT found that hysteroscopic exam prior to the procedure resulted in abnormalities being found in 43.3% of the 97 women in that study arm despite a normal ultrasound; pregnancy rates were higher for these women than for women not undergoing hysteroscopic exam (70.1% vs. 45.8%; OR 2.77 [95% CI, 1.53-5.00]).

In two other RCTs of women with a normal ultrasound undergoing IVF, hysteroscopy before IVF conferred no increase in live birth rate. In the inSIGHT trial, live births occurred in just over half of women in each group and in the TROPHY trial of women with 2 previous failed IVF attempts, live births occurred in just under one third in each group.

Clinicians should initiate work-up in women aged 35 to 40 years after 6 months of unprotected intercourse; for women over age 40 years, initiate work-up immediately. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommends specialist consultation if a woman has not conceived after 1 year of intercourse or after 6 cycles of artificial insemination, or earlier in certain circumstances; counselling should be offered before, during and after investigation and treatment for their fertility problems.

The initial work-up consists of a history and physical examination of both partners. For men, this includes family, social (e.g., exposures and relationship issues) and sexual history, prior fertility, genital examination, and sperm count. For women, this includes family, social, sexual and menstrual history, pelvic examination, and a screening endocrine evaluation. This chapter focuses on the evaluation of women.

The work-up for women should include screening for Chlamydia trachomatis, a day-3 FSH level, a day-23 serum progesterone level, a hysterosalpingogram, a pelvic ultrasound, and laboratory work as suggested by the history and physical examination (see ).

Although luteal phase deficiency, an abnormal luteal phase length of ≤10 days, has been associated with infertility, the condition is seen in fertile, normally menstruating women. Luteal phase deficiency has not been shown to be an independent entity causing infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss, and its treatment has not been shown to improve pregnancy outcomes.

Ovarian reserve testing using antral follicular count and anti-müllerian hormone can help identify women who may have a poor response or hyper responsiveness to ovarian stimulation for assisted reproductive technology. These tests were recommended by one author as having better predictive value than day-3 FSH level.
Women with infertility have low scores for quality of life and health-related quality of life and women and their partners may benefit from additional support.
Modest weight loss is beneficial for overweight women. B

First-line treatment for ovulation disorders is clomiphene; add metformin if unsuccessful. A Tamoxifen and letrozole are alternatives. A In women with PCOS, metformin was better than placebo for ovulation. B
Metformin and clomiphene are better than clomiphene alone for ovulation (OR 4.4) and pregnancy (OR 2.7), especially in clomiphene-resistant and obese women. A
For unexplained infertility, consider laparoscopy or trial of IUI or IUI with clomiphene. B.
Clomiphene or letrozole with IUI should be considered first-line therapy for unexplained infertility. A
If a woman is still not pregnant despite induced ovulation, consider laparoscopy, unstimulated IUI, IUI and clomiphene, gonadotropin injections with or without IUI, or IVF. C
Refer for IVF after 2 years of unexplained infertility or after 1 year of treatment for a particular defect. C IVF is not associated with an increased risk of breast cancer.

For anovulation, consider clomiphene citrate 25 to 50 mg starting on days 5 to 9 of the cycle; measure the serum progesterone on day 23. Clomiphene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM). If the patient is not ovulating, slowly increase the clomiphene dose in increments of 50 to 150 mg. Once ovulation is achieved, continue with the same dose for 3 months. Use of clomiphene is not associated with an increased risk of neural tube defects.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 28 clomiphene trials in women with PCOS found an increased chance of a clinical pregnancy compared with placebo (OR 5.91; 95% CI, 1.77-19.68) but no reports of live birth rates. A 10-day regimen may be more effective than a 5-day regimen.

A cohort study found a 4-fold increase in the rate of multiple gestations with the use of clomiphene citrate compared with no use. Other adverse pregnancy outcomes, including gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, miscarriage, and stillbirth, were also associated with clomiphene use, although the authors did not include an analysis to determine the strength of that association, or whether the association was due to medication use or the higher rate of multiple gestations.

In a secondary analysis of two RCTs including women who were overweight/obese and infertile with PCOS, women who received delayed treatment with clomiphene after preconception treatment with continuous oral contraceptives, lifestyle modification or both had higher rates of live birth compared to women treated immediately with four cycles of clomiphene (cumulative live birth rate: 25.0% for delayed treatment after lifestyle intervention only, 25.5% after lifestyle and oral contraceptive intervention, and 10.2% following 4 cycles of immediate clomiphene treatment).

Metformin alone or in combination with clomiphene is also used to treat anovulation. Metformin reduces blood sugar, in part, through reducing insulin resistance, which is present in women with PCOS. Metformin is started at 500 mg extended-release preparation with the evening meal. Every week, the dose is gradually increased to 2000 mg once daily. Metformin is stopped once pregnancy is achieved, although some continue the drug until after the first trimester.

However, metformin treatment before and during IVF or ICSI in women with PCOS versus placebo/no treatment did not clearly increase live birth rates based on 13 RCTs with 1132 women (live birth rate following placebo/no treatment was 28% vs. between 27% and 51% with metformin).
Letrozole, a third-generation aromatase inhibitor (AI), is also used to induce ovulation in women with PCOS. Letrozole leads to estrogen suppression which triggers FSH and ovulation.

In one RCT of 750 women with PCOS, women randomized to letrozole had more cumulative live births than those who received clomiphene (27.5% vs. 19.1%; rate ratio for live birth, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.10-1.87). There was a trend towards more major congenital anomalies in the letrozole group (4 vs. 1; p = 0.65) but no significant difference in pregnancy loss. More common adverse effects for letrozole were fatigue and dizziness; hot flushes were more common for women on clomiphene.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 57 trials with 8082 women concluded that both letrozole and combination clomiphene and metformin resulted in higher ovulation and pregnancy rates than clomiphene alone. Letrozole led to higher live birth rates compared to clomiphene alone (OR 1.67; 1.11-2.49) and both letrozole and metformin were associated with lower rates of multiple pregnancy than clomiphene alone. This finding was confirmed in a meta-analysis of RCTs in which pregnancy rate (29 studies with 3952 participants; 35% vs 23%; RR 1.5; 1.3 - 1.6) and live birth rate (8 studies with 1725 participants; 33% vs 22%; RR 1.5; 1.3 - 1.7) were higher with letrozole compared to clomiphene.

Tamoxifen, a SERM, can also be used for induction of ovulation. Tamoxifen appears comparable to clomiphene for live birth rate (22% vs. 21%-35%, respectively) based on two studies, but the Cochrane authors found insufficient data on clinical pregnancy rates of clomiphene plus tamoxifen over tamoxifen alone.

Vasodilators have been proposed to increase endometrial receptivity, thicken the endometrium, and favor uterine relaxation. Authors of a Cochrane review of 45 RCTs found insufficient evidence of an increase in live birth rate from use of vasodilators although there was some evidence of a positive effect on clinical pregnancy rates and adverse effects.

Sildenafil citrate increased endometrial thickness and improved the clinical pregnancy rate (risk ratio 1.3; 95% CI, 1.1-1.5) among infertile women with a thin endometrium based on a meta-analysis of 9 studies with 1452 patients.

Growth hormone has been used as adjuvant therapy for infertility. Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 trials found that growth hormone treatment in poor ovarian responders significantly increased the clinical pregnancy rate (OR 18, 95% CI, 1.2-2.5) but not the live birth rate.

Levothyroxine use during the preconception period and during pregnancy in euthyroid women who had thyroid peroxidase antibodies and a history of miscarriage or infertility did not result in higher rates of live births (37.4% vs. 37.9% in the placebo group) in one RCT of 952 women. Similarly, in an open-label RCT of 600 women undergoing IVF, use of levothyroxine in euthyroid women who had thyroid peroxidase antibodies did not reduce miscarriage rates (10.3% vs. 10.6% among control women) or improve live birth rates (31.7% vs. 32.3% in the control group).

Gonadotopins. Authors of a Cochrane review found higher pregnancy rates with gonadotrophins than anti-estrogens (OR 1.8, 95% CI, 1.2-2.7) based on 7 trials with 556 women. These authors advised low-dose protocols which result in similar pregnancy rates but minimize multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome; the latter occurs in approximately 3% to 8% of IVF cycles and consists of enlarged ovaries with multiple follicles causing acute fluid shift from intravascular space to third space and increased risk of thromboembolism and organ ischemia.
GnRH agonists resulted in a higher pregnancy rate among women with endometriosis-associated infertility based on a network meta-analysis (OR 1.68, 95% CI, 1.07-2.46).

Postoperative hormonal suppression with GnRH agonists may be considered in women wishing to conceive after surgery for endometriosis. A systemic review and meta-analysis reported increased chance of pregnancy with GnRH agonist use versus placebo or no treatment (RR 1.2, 95% CI 1.03-1.4), with increased chance of pregnancy when administered for at least 3 months (RR 1.2, 95% CI 1.04-1.4).

Among women with normogonadotropic anovulation who were not pregnant after six ovulatory cycles of clomiphene citrate, those randomized to gonadotrophins vs. continued clomiphene had higher live birth rates (52% vs. 41%); use of concomitant IUI did not influence outcomes.

Glucocorticoids. Glucocorticoids have been suggested as an aid in fertility treatment due to anti-inflammatory properties against the endometrium. It has been proposed that glucocorticoid administration after IVF or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) may suppress endometrial inflammation and enhance chances of embryo implantation. In a Cochrane review of 16 RCTs, the authors were uncertain if the use of peri-implantation glucocorticoids improved lived birth rates due to low-quality evidence (OR 1.4, 95% CI, 0.7-2.7).

list.listitem: In one study of 580 infertile women comparing clomiphene, IUI, and expectant management, live births occurred in a similar proportion in all 3 groups—14% for the clomiphene group, 23% for IUI, and 17% for the expectant management group. Women, however, preferred an active approach.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that fallopian tube sperm perfusion, which theoretically ensures higher sperm densities in the fallopian tubes at the time of ovulation, does not appear to be better than IUI with respect to safety or effectiveness for couples with non-tubal subfertility.

Based on the results of five trials, double IUI (two inseminations per cycle) with the husband's semen resulted in significant benefit over single IUI in the treatment of subfertile couples. Two other meta-analysis, one based on 6 RCTs and the other based on 9 studies of subferile women, however, failed to show outcome differences for live births.
Removal of cervical mucus prior to single-cycle IUI improved clinical pregnancy rates (31% vs. 21.8%) and live birth rates (26.9% vs. 18.7%) in one RCT.

In a trial of 201 women with unexplained infertility randomized to either IUI with ovarian stimulation or expectant management, women assigned to IUI had a higher cumulative live birth rate of 31% vs. 9%; the latter rate is lower than usually observed. Interestingly, 8 of the 31 women in the IUI group conceived without assistance or between IUI cycles and 2 of the 9 births in the expectant management group were the result of IUI or IVF.

Based on a secondary data analyses of an RCT of 900 women undergoing ovarian stimulation and IUI, a midluteal phase progesterone level >10th percentile specific for each treatment group (i.e., clomiphene, letrozole, or gonadotropin) was associated with greater odds for a live birth in all OS-IUI cycles (adjusted OR 2.17, 95% CI, 1.05-4.48).

Authors of a Cochrane review found that IUI resulted in improved live birth rates over cervical insemination in stimulated cycles using cryopreserved sperm for donor insemination. The timing of IUI (LH surge vs. hCG injection or time from hCG injection) did not appear to matter with respect to live birth rates.

Cochrane authors found no differences in live birth rates between different methods used for timing IUI or for guidance on the optimum time interval from hCG injection to IUI. Methods evaluated included hCG injection vs. LH surge, urinary hCG vs. recombinant hCG or hCG vs. GnRH agonist; study quality was poor.
In women with hyperprolactinemia undergoing IUI, the use of cabergoline was more effective than bromocriptine in achieving pregnancy (82% vs. 56.4%).

IVF can be considered for women with unexplained infertility (up to one third of cases). NICE recommends that women under age 40 years who are candidates be offered 3 full cycles of IVF while women aged 40 to 42 years be offered 12 full cycles. A full cycle of IVF involves collecting eggs and sperm, fertilizing the eggs outside the woman's body, and placing 1 or 2 fertilised eggs (embryos) into the uterus.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that IVF resulted in more live births per woman than expectant management (OR 22; 95% CI, 2.56-189.37; 2 trials); data quality was poor. In women pretreated with clomiphene + IUI, IVF appears to result in higher birth rates than IUI + gonadotropins. However, in women who are treatment-naïve, there is no conclusive evidence of a difference in live birth rates between IVF and IUI + gonadotropins or between IVF and IUI + clomiphene.

Authors of a Cochrane review found recombinant FSH was slightly better than urinary FSH for ovulatory stimulation in assisted reproduction cycles (OR for clinical pregnancy per cycle 1.21 [1.04, 1.42]; absolute increase in clinical pregnancy rate with rFSH is 3.7% [0.8, 6.7]).

In an RCT of 1508 infertile women with PCOS undergoing IVF, embryo cryopreservation followed by frozen-embryo transfer resulted in higher percentages of live birth after the first transfer than fresh-embryo transfer (49.3% vs. 42.0%). However, in an RCT of 782 women with infertility and no PCOS, ongoing pregnancy after a single cycle did not differ based on type of embryo transferred (36.3% in the frozen-embryo group and 34.5% in the fresh-embryo group). Similarly, among ovulatory women with infertility, live birth rate did not differ significantly between fresh-embryo transfer and frozen-embryo transfer (48.7% and 50.2%, respectively), although frozen-embryo transfer resulted in a lower risk of the ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
Use of a single 20 mg dose of nifedipine 30 minutes prior to embryo transfer did not improve the implantation rate or clinical pregnancy rate in one RCT.

Adjunctive glucocorticoid treatment was helpful for infertile women who were antithyroid antibody (ATA)-positive vs. ATA-negative and undergoing assisted reproductive technology for both improving clinical pregnancy rate (OR 4.63, 95% CI, 2.23-9.58) and live birth rate (OR 3.19, 95% CI, 1.13-9.04). Authors of a Cochrane review, however, found insufficient evidence that routine administration of peri‐implantation glucocorticoids in subfertile women during IVF/ICSI cycles influenced clinical outcomes.

Among subfertile women undergoing IVF, it was unclear if administration of granulocyte-colony stimulating factor improved overall clinical pregnancy or ongoing pregnancy compared to no treatment or placebo based on a review of 15 trials with 622 patients; data on live birth rates were not reported.
ICSI is a technique in which a single sperm is injected into an egg to achieve fertilization.

The American Society for Reproductive Medicine concluded that ICSI for women with unexplained fertility is associated with increased fertilization rates but not improved live-birth rates. They concluded that ICSI without male factor infertility may be of benefit for select patients undergoing IVF with preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disease and previously cryo-preserved oocytes. NICE recommends ICSI for women having IVF only if there are severe deficits in semen quality, obstructive azoospermia, non obstructive azoospermia or if previous IVF treatment resulted in failed or very poor fertilization.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies concluded no difference between IVF and ICSI for live birth rates among infertile patients due to non-male factors (RR 0.94, 95% CI, 0.82-1.07); clinical pregnancy rates favored IVF.

As noted above, based on 16 RCTs, Cochrane authors were unable to determine if administration of peri-implantation glucocorticoids for women undergoing IVF or ICSI significantly improved pregnancy or live birth rates. Conclusions were based on very low to low-certainty evidence with the main limitations of serious risk of bias, poor methods reporting and serious imprecision.
In one large RCT, use of hyaluronan-selected sperm vs. standard ICSI did not result in higher term live birth rates (27.4% vs. 25.2%, respectively).

For women with PCOS, although use of metformin prior to or during IVF or ICSI cycles improved clinical pregnancy rates, there was no conclusive evidence that metformin treatment improved live birth rates. The risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome was lower and risk of side effects higher in the metformin vs. placebo groups.

For women at risk of developing ovarian hyperstimulation during IVF/ICSI treatment, one RCT of 200 women demonstrated that intravenous calcium infusion reduced the incidence of ovarian hyperstimulation without reducing the pregnancy rate.
There are only a small number of clinical trials of tubal surgery for infertility, and only one comparing it with no treatment or sham treatment.

For intrauterine disease, consider operative hysteroscopy. In a meta-analysis of 8 studies including 3 RCTs for women with recurrent implantation failure, use of hysteroscopy before the IVF cycle improved clinical pregnancy rates but not live birth rates. For women with a septate uterus, hysteroscopic septoplasty resulted in a 45% live birth rate in pooled studies. Authors of a Cochrane review found 1 RCT and 12 non-randomized trials to evaluate septoplasty. The RCT found no evidence to suggest an increase in live births (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.32-2.11). It is not known whether removal of endometrial polyps improves fertility.

Similarly, data are limited regarding the benefits of myomectomy on subsequent fertility or live birth. In fact, it has not been clearly established that fibroids are associated with infertility, and studies comparing women with and without fibroids, found no significant difference in time to pregnancy (1.9; 95% CI 0.9 to 4.2).
For tubal blockage distally, consider operative laparoscopy. For tubal blockage proximally, consider interventional radiology to relieve obstruction.

HSG with water-soluble media can act as a "tubal flush," with some evidence of effectiveness for infertility. Authors of a Cochrane review found uncertain benefit based on a single trial of water-soluble contrast media, but an increase in live births following tubal flushing with oil‐soluble contrast media vs. no treatment (OR 3.27, 95% CI, 1.57 -6.85, 3 RCTs, 204 women) and vs. water-soluble contrast media (OR 1.64, 95% CI, 1.27-2.11, 1119 women from two trials).
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling for PCOS shows results as good as those with metformin.

Laparoscopy for unexplained infertility has been used to evaluate for endometriosis and/or adhesions involving the tubes or ovaries or impaired ovum transport. For women with endometriosis-associated infertility, laparoscopy was associated with higher odds of pregnancy (OR 1.6, 95% CI, 1.1-2.4).

While there is evidence that use of an absorbable adhesion barrier (Interceed) reduced the incidence of adhesion formation following laparoscopy and laparotomy, there are insufficient data to support its use to improve pregnancy rates.

For proximal tubal occlusion, consult an interventional radiologist. There is insufficient evidence to support use of hydrotubation or second-look laparoscopy following female pelvic reproductive surgery.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found acupuncture more effective than clomiphene citrate for women with anovulatory infertility with respect to pregnancy rate (OR 2.3, 95% CI, 1.8-3.1), but no differences in outcomes when acupuncture was used as adjunctive therapy.

Data are conflicting on benefits of acupuncture for women with infertility undergoing IVF. In a Cochrane review of this topic, acupuncture performed on the day of embryo transfer had a beneficial effect on the live birth rate; however, the evidence was based on a single trial and the finding could be attributed to placebo effect.

In an RCT of 114 women undergoing in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer, application of acupuncture and moxibustion had some influence on biochemical parameters but did not affect the clinical pregnancy rate.

In a recent RCT of 72 women with infertility undergoing IVF, women randomized to 3 sessions of acupuncture before and after embryo transfer had reduced anxiety levels and significantly increased the pregnancy and live birth rates compared to the placebo group (19/36 vs. 10/36 for live birth).
However, for trials using placebo acupuncture, there was no benefit of therapeutic acupuncture on IVF outcomes based on a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs including 3607 patients.
In a 4-arm RCT of 1000 Chinese women with infertility and PCOS, active acupuncture with or without clomiphene did not improve live birth rates compared to sham treatment.
Chinese herbal medicine in combination with IVF was more effective in increasing live birth rates over IVF alone (RR 1.3, 95% CI, 1.05-1.7), based on a systematic review of RCTs.

Deep relaxation massage using oscillating vibrations (andullation therapy) delivered over 30 minutes prior to embryo transfer in IVF cryo-cycles prior to blastocyst transfer resulted in higher pregnancy rates (58.9% vs. 41.7%) and birth rates (32.0% vs. 20.3%) for women randomized to treatment vs. control women.

Discontinue or avoid smoking, alcohol, illicit drugs, and toxins both in the home and at work. In general, however, preconception lifestyle advice appears to have little to no influence on number of live births based on a Cochrane review of 7 RCTs involving 2130 participants.

There is a positive association between psychosocial interventions, in particular long-duration interventions, and pregnancy rate in infertile women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (RR 1.2, CI 1.04-1.4).
Have regular intercourse every 2 to 3 days, especially 5 to 6 days before expected ovulation.
Weight loss can result in resumption of ovulation. Metformin was as successful as sibutramine or orlistat for weight reduction.
N-acetyl-cysteine, as adjuvant therapy, was not effective in improving outcomes based on a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs with 2330 subjects.

Based on a review of 3 observational cohort studies, supplemental folic acid, particularly at doses higher than those recommended for the prevention of neural tube defects, is associated with lower frequency of infertility, lower risk of pregnancy loss, and greater success in infertility treatment.

In a Danish cohort study of 3895 women planning pregnancy, the fecundability rate (FR) was increased among women taking a folic acid supplement (FR 1.2, 95% CI, 1.06-1.). Among 232 women undergoing assisted reproduction, higher folate intake was associated with higher rates of implantation, clinical pregnancy, and live birth; for the latter, live birth occurred for 30% (95% CI, 21%-42%) of women in the lowest quartile of folate intake to 56% (95% CI 43%-67%) in the highest quartile.
Of note, folic acid and zinc supplementation for male partners does not improve semen quality or increase live birth rates.

No overall increased risk of breast cancer was found following infertility treatment in a cohort of Swedish women, but women treated with high-dose clomiphene citrate appeared to be at increased risk (standardized incidence ratio 1.9; 95% CI, 1.08-3.4). Authors of a meta-analysis of cohort studies confirmed no increased risk of breast cancer with use of clomiphene citrate and gonadotropins in infertile women.

An umbrella review (a meta-analysis of meta-analyses) found a weak association between a history of treatment for female infertility and later ovarian cancer (OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.00-1.45). IVF had the strongest association (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.07-2.54), but clomiphene also had a small positive association.
In one study, there was an increased incidence of preeclampsia in pregnancies resulting from donor sperm vs. partner insemination group: 10.9% (48/438) vs. 7.2% (20/275).

IVF is associated with a small but significant increased risk of intellectual disability (less than 7 per 100,000 person-years) compared with spontaneous conception. The risk of autism was not increased.
After 3 years of unprotected intercourse, 94% of fertile women age 35 years and 77% who are 38 years old will conceive. B
About half of couples conceive after the first year of infertility. B

In a Belgian study of outcomes of donor insemination for various indications, cumulative delivery rates after 12 cycles were 87% for the group aged 20 to 29 years, 77% for ages 30 to 34 years, 76% for ages 35 to 37 years, 66% for ages 38 to 39 years, and 52% for ages 40 to 45 years. B

In a Canadian registry of 8195 IVF cycles using ICSI and the women's own oocytes, the clinical pregnancy rate per cycle was 32.1% and the live birth rate was 25.6%; multiple birth rate per delivery was 30.8%. In 301 IVF/ICSI cycles using donor oocytes, the clinical pregnancy rate was 46.5%, and the live birth rate was 35.2%; the multiple birth rate was 33.3%. In 2498 frozen embryo transfer cycles using the woman's own oocytes, the clinical pregnancy rate was 22.8%, and the live birth rate was 17.4%; the multiple birth rate was 24.5%.

In a population-based UK cohort study of IVF including 113, 873 women with 184 ,269 complete cycles, 29.1% had a live birth after their first complete cycle and 43% after six complete cycles. Two pretreatment predictors of live birth were identified—age (31 years vs. 37 years; adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.7; 95% CI, 1.6-1.7) and duration of infertility (3 years vs. 6 years; OR 1.1; 95% CI, 1.08-1.1). Post-treatment predictors were number of eggs collected (13 vs. 5 eggs; OR 1.3; 95% CI, 1.3-1.32), cryopreservation of embryos (OR 1.9; 95% CI, 1.9-1.96), age (OR 1.5; 95% CI, 1.5-1.6), and stage of embryos transferred (e.g., double blastocyst vs. double cleavage; OR 1.8; 95% CI, 1.7-1.9).
Among women undergoing IVF, the presence of bacterial vaginosis was associated with early spontaneous abortion (RR 1.7, 95% CI, 1.2-2.3) but did not influence the live birth rate.

Among 359 women with endometriosis undergoing assistive reproductive technology in one case series, 44% became pregnant, and 31.8% had a live birth. Factors associated with poor outcomes were history of past surgery for endometriosis and anti-müllerian hormone levels <2 ng/mL and antral follicle count <10.

For women undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation and IUI in one study, all women with an FSH of 10 to 15 mIU/mL and E2 ≥40 pg/mL on day 3 testing failed to achieve live birth after treatment. IVF was successful for 6 of 18 couples.
If 4 years have elapsed, the prognosis is poor; consider referral to adoption service.

Authors of a literature review concluded that children born following IUI/IVF had no increased risk of birth defects or significant differences in growth, development or cognitive function compared with naturally-conceived children. There was some evidence that IVF-conceived children had lower birth weights, higher blood pressure and higher fasting glucose concentrations than naturally-conceived children.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies comparing 3972 children born after IVF/ICSI with 11,012 spontaneously-conceived children found no statistically significant difference in child weight or height by age 5 years.
Infertility for 4 years or more has a poor prognosis.
Consider referral to adoption services.
Stop smoking, avoid all toxins, and begin folic acid 1 mg per day.
Check for varicella and rubella antibody status; consider vaccinating before conception.
Optimize pre-conception BMI through dietary and lifestyle modifications.
